steps.body: One more family of equivalents: **2/2, 5/5, 9/9 all land on the same spot — 1.** And it keeps going: six third-jumps land on 2, so 6/3 = 2. Whole numbers wear fraction costumes, and the number line unmasks every one.

widget.prompt: This line runs 0→3, cut into THIRDS (9 jumps in all). Slide to 6/3.
widget.lowFeedback: Keep jumping — every 3 third-jumps banks another whole.
widget.highFeedback: Too far — you've jumped past the sixth jump. Slide back.
widget.successFeedback: Six third-jumps: two complete trips of three. 6/3 lands exactly on 2 — a whole number in costume.

predict.prompt: You'll slide to 6/3 on a line that runs 0→3. Where will 6/3 land?
predict.reveal: Every 3 third-jumps banks one whole — six jumps banks exactly two wholes, so 6/3 sits right on 2.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents whole as fraction.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for whole as fraction must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines whole as fraction.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

explanationVariants: Four fourth-jumps make each whole, so three wholes take 12 jumps: 12/4 = 3.
Bank the wholes: 4/4 is 1, 8/4 is 2, 12/4 is 3.

options.feedback: Twelve fourth-jumps at four per whole: three wholes, on the nose.
3/4 hasn't even finished the FIRST whole — it's one jump short of 1. Three wholes need 12 fourth-jumps.
4/3 is one whole plus a single third — just past 1. The number 3 in thirds would be 9/3 (or 12/4 in fourths).
Top equals bottom lands on 1, always — 3/3 is 1 in costume, not 3.

steps.body: Here's a secret handshake with division: **6/3 can be read as '6 shared by 3.'** Six third-pieces, grouped three-per-whole, make 2 — and 6 ÷ 3 = 2 as well. Same answer, no accident. The fraction bar is a quiet division sign.

explanationVariants: Four fourths per whole: eight fourths bank exactly two wholes — 8/4 = 2.
Read the bar as division: 8 shared by 4 is 2.

commonErrors.feedback: 4 is the bottom — the jump size. Count the wholes instead: four fourths per whole, and you have eight of them.
32 multiplied the two numbers — but the bar isn't a times sign. Read it as sharing: 8 shared by 4.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Every 4 fourth-jumps is one whole — count how many wholes 8 jumps make.

widget.prompt: Build a fraction costume for the number 2, using SIXTHS.

commonBuilds.feedback: 2/6 is a small piece — two sixth-jumps, a third of ONE trip. The number 2 needs two complete trips: 12 sixths.
6/6 is 1 — one full trip of sixths. The number 2 is a second trip further: 12/6.

widget.missFeedback: Six sixths per whole — two wholes need twice that on top.
widget.successFeedback: 12/6 = 2: six sixth-jumps per whole, twelve for two. Costume fitted.

explanationVariants: Five fifth-pieces are ALL the pieces — together they rebuild the whole exactly: 5/5 = 1.
On the line: five jumps of a five-jump trip is the complete trip, landing on 1.

options.label: Five fifth-pieces are every piece of the whole — together they rebuild it exactly
options.feedback: All the pieces, all the trip — top matching bottom means nothing is missing.

options.label: The fives cancel out and disappear
options.feedback: True answer, risky reason — nothing vanishes. The five pieces are all still there; together they ARE the whole. The model beats the magic.

options.label: Because 5 + 5 = 10
options.feedback: Adding top to bottom mixes the two jobs. The 5s match — meaning every one of the five pieces is taken: one whole.

options.label: It doesn't — 5/5 is five
options.feedback: Five FIFTH-jumps only cover one trip — 5/5 stands exactly on 1. The number five would be 25/5.

hints: How many fourths make ONE whole?
Four per whole — and you need three wholes.
explanationVariants: Four fourths per whole, three wholes: 3 × 4 = 12 fourths — so 3 = 12/4.
Bank them on the line: 4/4 is 1, 8/4 is 2, 12/4 is 3.

widget.prompt: Write the number 3 in fourths: 3 = ?/4. Enter the top number.

commonErrors.feedback: 3/4 copies the whole number on top — but that's three-quarters, less than ONE whole. Each whole costs 4 fourths.
7 added 3 and 4 — the plus-both-numbers reflex again. Wholes come in groups of four fourths: 3 groups of 4.

widget.fallbackFeedback: One whole = 4 fourths. Three wholes = three groups of that.

takeaways: n/n always lands on 1 — all the pieces rebuild the whole.
Count wholes in groups: b jumps per whole, so 12/4 banks three wholes.
The fraction bar reads as sharing: 6/3 is 6 shared by 3.
steps.teaser: the finale: comparing fractions — same bottoms, same tops, and the one rule that guards them all.

concept.body: Quick rewind. Count wholes out loud while jumping in fourths: **"4/4 — one! 8/4 — two! 12/4 — three!"** Every time the top collects another full set of the bottom, you've banked another whole.

explanationVariants: Five fifths per whole: ten fifths bank two wholes — 10/5 = 2.
Read it as sharing: 10 shared by 5 is 2.

options.feedback: Two full sets of five fifths — two wholes.
5 is the jump size (the bottom). Count the SETS: ten fifths is two sets of five — 2.
50 multiplied — but the bar shares instead: 10 shared by 5 is 2.
